text: I guess the simple answer is that Saturn's moons are the interesting places to check for life later, so we didn't want Cassini accidentally knocking into one and leaving Earth dust or microbes behind. By the end, Cassini had too little fuel to do a safe, controlled landing on Enceladus or Titan. Hitting Saturn's atmosphere meant it would burn up, which is a much cleaner way to retire it than risking a stray impact with a moon. That's why the final dive into Saturn was the safer bet. It makes sense when you think about how careful planetary scientists are about not messing with potentially habitable worlds.

Usually it’s not the fact that the leg is stationary. It’s what you’re doing to keep it there. When you’re cruising, the non-pushing leg is still doing quiet work: your ankle is absorbing small bumps, your knee is slightly bent, and your hip is holding your balance. If your stance is a little off, that leg ends up carrying more of the shock than the pushing leg, so the muscles and joints get sore fast. If you’re locking your knee or gripping the deck too hard, the shock goes straight up the shin and knee. That’s a common source of pain for people who don’t realize their posture is doing the work.

I’d guess you’re putting your weight too far back or too far forward, or standing with your feet in an awkward position that forces the stationary leg to brace. A small change, like keeping your knees loose and your shoulders over your feet, usually helps. It can also be fatigue: even the leg that looks still is contracting constantly to keep you upright, and after a while that tiredness shows up as an ache.

Honestly, most skaters get some aching in the non-pushing leg if their balance is sloppy. It’s easier to blame the pushing leg, but the quiet leg is often doing more than you think. If the pain is sharp, or only in one spot, it’s worth checking whether you’re landing hard or riding with a bent knee. For a lot of people, the fix is simple: relax the stance, bend the knees a bit more, and don’t try to push too hard with one leg for too long. You don’t have to ride fast to make this better; cleaner balance usually takes the strain off that stationary leg.

I think the confusion comes from assuming “African American” means people are actually from Africa right now. It’s really about ancestry. Most Black Americans trace their roots to people who were taken from the continent, often under the slave trade, so the term is a way of acknowledging that heritage, not their current address. I’d say most of them are not currently from Africa, and that’s true, but a lot of the word points to where their families started, not where they live.

I mean, some Black Americans do come from Africa, of course, but the label isn’t trying to make everyone from there. It’s more about shared cultural and historical connections. And honestly, “Afro-American” isn’t as common as “African American” in everyday usage. I’ve also seen people use it loosely, which probably adds to the mix-up. For me it’s less about geography and more about lineage. Even if someone was born in New York or Boston, the term still reaches back to West or Central Africa in many cases, though not every family can point to a specific village. The point isn’t that everyone in the US who is Black is from Africa; it’s that their families often have deep African roots.

I think the "all drugs are bad" idea comes from seeing the worst cases, not from pharmacology. Not all drugs are bad; some are lifesaving, and small doses of recreational drugs can be fine for some people. But the reason people lump them together is that drugs acting directly on the reward system create a strong incentive to take more. Heroine and cocaine both make the brain's reward circuitry fire, and once that happens, the body starts adapting. Tolerance means you need more to get the same effect, and when you stop, the system is left under-stimulated, which is what withdrawal is. So even if the molecule itself did almost no damage, the effect on homeostasis is the problem. You can imagine a drug that gives intense euphoria with a hard ceiling, so you can't take too much. That solves overdose, but not the deeper issue: your brain's set point shifts. If the drug is that good, you want it constantly, and constant activation changes how you feel when you're not taking it. That's the trade-off with pleasure drugs. They're not just chemicals that make you feel good; they also tell your body to stop making its own good-feeling chemicals. So zero adverse effects is almost a contradiction in terms. Every drug has some effect on some system, and strong effects leave marks. So it's hard to imagine a heroin-level high with no trace. Even a chemically gentle drug hitting the reward pathway will get the brain adapting. The stronger the high, the stronger the pull to keep taking it. The answer isn't that all drugs are bad, it's that intense pleasure drugs are especially likely to change the brain's baseline. You get high, then the baseline drops below normal, then you need the drug just to feel okay. That's the hidden cost. It's also why "zero adverse effects" is hard: if there are no side effects at all, the drug is probably not doing much. Strong effect means strong system involvement, and system involvement means the system rebalances. I'd be cautious about the idea of a perfect pleasure drug. It might exist in theory, but biology resists free gifts. The reward system isn't designed to be overloaded without consequences. So a drug with intense euphoria and no adverse effects would be like finding a free meal that also fixes your blood pressure and mood. It's not impossible, but it's a very high bar.

Hi,
Thanks for writing. I think you said “milk” because the little repetition game left you a bit scattered, and when he asked what cows drink, your brain reached for the most familiar association. Cows and milk are so tightly connected in everyday language that the expected answer can slip out before the actual fact gets a chance. It’s not really a memory failure; it’s more like your attention was still caught up in the previous task. I’ve had the same kind of mix-up myself, where the obvious cultural link is stronger than the technical answer. Honestly, it’s a funny example of how context can hijack a simple question. If I had to guess, you were still mentally finishing the silk repetition, and his next question landed while you were in a low-attention mode. I mean, it’s not that you forgot water. Your brain just took the shortcut.
Take care,
Me

Hey,

You're in the right mindset for house hunting if you're asking these questions early. I'm not an agent, but here's what I'd want to know before putting money down: get a mortgage pre-approval, because it tells you your real budget. Then look at the property itself, not the listing photos. I'd check for water damage, cracks, weird smells, and whether the seller has any disclosure documents. Also ask about utilities and taxes. Those surprise people. Don't forget movers.

I'd also be suspicious of a home that's too cheap for the neighborhood. That usually means the seller is hiding something or rushing the sale. If you can, get a professional inspection. It's not expensive and it can save you from a bigger problem later.

Before signing, make sure the contract lets you walk away if financing falls through or the inspection finds issues. Also ask the seller why they're moving. Sometimes that tells you a lot.

And take the area at different times of day. Traffic, noise, parking, and how it feels at night all matter.

Don't rush, but don't overthink. Make a short list of what you actually need, and let the rest be flexible.

Alex

Hey Sam,

I was actually just thinking about this the other day. Honestly, the main difference is that a 3-in-1 is just a compromise. You're basically mixing cleaning agents meant for skin with ones meant for hair, and you're getting the worst of both worlds sometimes. 

Shampoo needs stronger surfactants to cut through scalp oil, while body wash is much milder for your skin. When you use a 3-in-1, it's usually too harsh for your face and arms, or it just doesn't have enough conditioning agents to keep your hair soft. A 2-in-1 is a step up for hair, but it still lacks the specific pH balance and deep conditioning of a real conditioner. I mean, a 3-in-1 sounds like a great idea, but in practice it's mostly just a diluted version of a standard shampoo with a tiny bit of skin moisturizer tossed in. 

I use them sometimes when I'm lazy or traveling, but my hair ends up feeling dry and my skin feels a bit stripped. I've noticed my scalp gets flaky when I use them too often. I think it's mostly a convenience thing, and maybe even a marketing trick to get you to buy one bottle instead of three. Plus, your hair and skin just need different environments, and a single product can't perfectly satisfy both. 

Anyway, let me know what you think. 

Talk soon,
Alex

Hi Sam,

Funny you ask that. The short answer is GPS, but it's not just one reading. Surveyors put up fixed GPS stations on continental plates and record their positions over months or years. By comparing where a station was, say, a year ago with where it is now, they can work out a speed in millimetres per year. That's how they say a continent is drifting a few centimetres each year, roughly the length of a fingernail in a month. Of course, no single station tells the whole story. They use networks of stations, and they check that nearby points move consistently. Earthquakes or local settling can throw off one reading, so the networks smooth things out.

There are other checks too. Satellite radar can pick up ground deformation, and older evidence like fossil matches, rock strata and magnetic striping on the sea floor supports the big picture. GPS is the direct, modern measurement; the geological record is what lets you extrapolate much farther back in time. I find it wild that a whole landmass is moving at fingernail-growth speed. It feels too slow to feel, but add up the years and the continents really do shuffle around.

Best,
You

Think of it like inherited genetic baggage. IQ is not controlled by one gene; it's influenced by many small genetic effects plus environment. When relatives have children, they share more of the same ancestors, so the child is more likely to get two copies of the same rare harmful variant. If the variant is recessive, it usually stays hidden in a single copy, but with related parents it can appear as a pair and show up. That increases the chance of inbreeding depression: the family carries more hidden problems, and the offspring express more of them. The drop in average IQ is a population-level pattern, not a guarantee for every child. Close relatives can still have perfectly healthy kids, but the statistical risk is higher. The bigger the family tree overlap, the bigger the effect. That's why families where parents are related often see a measurable dip in cognitive test averages.

I'd guess it's mostly about where the pain receptors are. The arm isn't pain free; a cut, shot or hit can still be quite sharp. But compared with the hand, chest or face, the arm usually has a lower density of pain receptors in the skin and soft tissue, so the same kind of injury may register as less intense. We also tend to move the arm away and shield it. Adrenaline during a sudden injury can blunt the signal too. That doesn't mean you can ignore it. If it hits a nerve, tendon, bone or joint, the pain can be much worse. My takeaway for a new colleague is that the arm often seems less painful because it's less sensitive, and because we can move it away from the body. So what matters is the location of the receptors and how bad the wound is, not just the arm itself.

Honestly, I think the best way to look at this is to think about what your blood is actually doing. Carbon dioxide isn't really a poison; it's just your body's normal metabolic waste. You're constantly making it, and your lungs are basically a clearinghouse designed to expel it. You only get sick from CO2 if the concentration gets ridiculously high, like in a sealed room where you're breathing it in faster than you can breathe it out. At everyday levels, it's just part of normal breathing. But carbon monoxide is a totally different beast.

I'd guess the biggest issue with CO is what it does to your hemoglobin. Your red blood cells have these proteins that are supposed to grab oxygen and carry it around to your tissues. Carbon monoxide hangs onto that hemoglobin about two hundred times tighter than oxygen does. So if you breathe it in, it crowds out the oxygen, and your brain and organs start starving for it. You don't even get a warning sign, because it's completely invisible and odorless. That's why it's so sneaky. I mean, your body isn't built to fight it off easily, so you can just slowly lose consciousness before you can do anything about it. I've always found that pretty terrifying, and it’s why people get caught off guard. I suppose it's the tight binding that makes it so dangerous, since your body doesn't realize the oxygen transport is compromised until it's too late. The brain is super sensitive to oxygen deprivation, so you get headaches, confusion, and dizziness first. It's a weird one, because CO2 is just your body's own exhaust, whereas CO is an outsider that completely jams your delivery system. And because it binds so tightly, it takes a lot of pure oxygen to wash it out, which is why hospitals use those big oxygen tents.

In an aircraft emergency, the brace position is a simple way to protect yourself from the sudden movement of a crash or hard landing. The idea is not to hold your breath or freeze, but to get your body into a stable, compact shape before impact.

Normally, when an aircraft stops very quickly, your body keeps moving forward or backward because of inertia. If you are not bracing, your head, chest and limbs can strike the seat, the floor or other passengers. The brace position reduces that risk. You keep your head down and hands in front or over your head, bend your knees and stay low against the seat or a fixed point. This makes it harder for your body to lurch around.

It also helps by spreading the force over your legs and arms rather than concentrating it in your spine or skull. For a new colleague, the key point is that bracing is not a magic shield; it just keeps you more stable and protected during the few seconds before impact. In practice, you follow the crew's instructions, keep your feet flat and your back against the seat, and avoid trying to move your arms or legs too much.

There are old trading houses and guilds, but the names we recognize today mostly date from the industrial era or later. Before factories and global supply chains, businesses were smaller, family-run and region-bound, so their reputations rarely spread far. Many were absorbed, renamed or folded into larger firms during industrialization. A company's survival also depended on succession and local politics, not on the marketing machines and brand systems that only became common after industry took hold. So the absence of famous pre-industrial brands isn't evidence that old businesses didn't exist; it reflects how much the modern economy changed what "well known" even means.

I got the same feeling the first time I saw a dealer's rate look better than my bank's, so I tried to figure out why the bank still won on total cost. For me it comes down to what is actually in the loan, not the sticker APR. A dealership can quote 3 percent on a $30,000 car and still charge a lot of things on top: a doc fee, a dealer admin fee, a market adjustment, and optional extras like extended warranties or service packages. If those extras are financed into the loan, you end up paying interest on money you did not really need to borrow. My bank did not do that. It simply made a loan on the car, with a small origination fee, and no pushy extras.

That is the point I keep coming back to. The headline rate is only part of the story. A dealer can use a low rate as bait, then load up the deal with products. The low rate may make the monthly payment look attractive, while the total amount financed grows because of fees and extras. In other words, a lower rate does not guarantee a cheaper deal. I have seen deals where the dealer's advertised rate was low, but the payment included a big bundle of extras that I did not want. The bank's higher rate was less tempting at first glance, but the total cost was lower because there were fewer hidden charges and no upsell built into the loan.

I would also point out that dealer financing can include holdback and other dealer side money, and that dealer extras are often sold as protection. I was not asking for an extended warranty. I just wanted the car and a fair loan. My bank gave me that. I think the real reason is transparency. A bank is less interested in selling me extras, so I got a cleaner loan. The dealer had an incentive to make the purchase price and loan package bigger. That is why, for me, the bank was cheaper even though its rate was not the lowest quoted rate. It was the total cost that mattered, not just the percentage.

I am not saying dealers always overcharge. Some are fair, and some banks charge high fees. But I would not trust the low dealer rate on its own. I would add up every fee and product, then compare total repayments. That is how I ended up with a lower bill through my bank, despite the dealer's better sounding rate.

I think strongly that states should get to decide for themselves about marijuana, but the reality is messier than anyone wants to admit. Right now, a handful of states have legalized recreational use, while others allow it only for medical purposes, and still others haven't moved at all. I keep getting frustrated by how uneven this is. I live in a state where you can buy weed at a licensed shop, but driving twenty miles in another direction puts you in a state where it's still illegal. To me, the state-by-state patchwork is less about policy and more about politics and money. I think we're closer to nationwide agreement than people admit, but the gap between what's legal, what's medical-only, and what's still banned is wide enough to confuse tourists, drivers, and people who just want a beer and a joint on a weekend. I'm not sure the federal government will step in soon.

I keep picturing electricity in the body as some hidden lightning, but honestly it's much more like tiny voltage differences built from ions. Our cells pump sodium out and potassium in, so the inside of a nerve cell stays negative compared with the outside. When a signal needs to fire, channels open, sodium rushes in, the cell briefly flips positive, and that quick change travels down the axon. That is the "spark" we mean. The same ion flow lets muscle fibers contract. So the body doesn't store big charges; it maintains gradients and releases them in controlled bursts.

I keep coming back to one idea when people ask how musicians sample older songs: the interesting part isn’t the legal stuff, it’s the hunting. If you’ve ever sat down with a crate of old records, you know what I mean. You’re not just listening for a good song. You’re listening for the three or four seconds where the song does something weird, a drum fill, a vocal ad-lib, a broken horn stab, a crackle and hiss that you can’t get from a clean digital file. That’s the real craft.

A lot of people think sampling is mostly about copyright and permission. It is part of it, but that’s the part you deal with later, if you ever need to release commercially. The first act is choosing material. Some producers dig for obscure recordings from the 60s or 70s because the imperfections are part of the appeal. A scratched record, a tape hiss, a slightly off-key line, those things give the sample its texture. A clean MIDI note doesn’t have that.

Then comes the flip. This is where a sample stops being a copy and starts being a new idea. You might take a melodic phrase from an old soul record, slow it down, run it through a bitcrusher, and use it as a bassline instead of a melody. Or you chop a drum break into slices and rearrange the order so it becomes a rhythm pattern. The point isn’t to reproduce the original; it’s to make the fragment serve a new song.

I’ve watched this happen in the studio. Someone finds a five-second loop, loops it, then keeps cutting it into smaller pieces and changing their pitch until it sounds like something that could have existed on its own. That’s where the “how” becomes less technical and more musical. You’re not just using a snippet; you’re rebuilding it.

There’s also the question of whether that’s fair use or just borrowing. Honestly, the line is fuzzy. Some producers get lucky, some get sued, and some pay for licenses. But in the creative moment, a lot of it is about instinct. You hear something in a 1972 record and think, “This little bit could be the hook of my next track.” The sample becomes a seed, not a finished piece.

I used to think headaches meant my actual brain was hurting, but I’ve come to believe it’s mostly the stuff around the brain. The brain itself doesn’t really feel pain, so the pain signals come from the meninges, blood vessels, and nerves in the head. For me, it usually starts as a dull, heavy pressure behind my eyes, then tightens around my temples. I notice it after I’ve been staring at a screen too long, slept badly, or skipped a meal. It’s not just ‘sick head’ in a vague way; there are physical triggers and pathways. My guess is that stress and dehydration make the blood vessels and nerves around the brain more reactive, which is why the pain can feel like a band squeezing my skull. I still don’t know the exact reason for mine, but knowing it’s the surrounding tissues, not the brain itself, makes it feel less mysterious.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m. Surprisingly, there wasn't a single person in line. The total for two people came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep to me. Before we went in, I figured the price would be comparable to what you'd pay at a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually costs somewhat more than I had expected to pay at one.

Honestly, I was really disappointed that they didn't offer steak. At that price, I fully assumed there would be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are the kind of things I feel like you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for a lot less money.

The seafood station was the only part that really stood out. It had Alaskan crab legs, which are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were definitely interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I really didn't want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and various pastries, but nothing there really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any of them.

Overall, I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. If you hit it with the edge of your thumb, it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so “example” ends up as “eexample” and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, and only when I’m typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I’d already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don’t ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I’d have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little closer to the middle now.

I’ve been going to Vegas my whole life, the under-21 version of it, so I’ve sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and honestly? Mixed. Maybe slightly worse than mixed.

First, the good: the circular stage is genuinely smart. You’re looking down into it, so from essentially any seat you get a decent view. That’s rare in Vegas. Some acts are impressive. The strength stuff, the aerialists, the divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a “rip-off” way exactly, just... if you’ve seen Cirque, you’ve seen comparable feats done with maybe more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What is the story? I still don’t know. There’s a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it’s trying to say. Also, there’s way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like the stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing, more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you’re staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal. $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn’t pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn’t blown away, and I don’t think anyone else was either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you’ve never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don’t expect to leave overwhelmed.

Around two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father from Rockmount Ranch Wear over the phone. They never arrived. The sales rep got the delivery address wrong. Her handwritten 7 was read as a 1, so 5407 became 5401. The people at 5401 brought the package to the local UPS store to send it back. Then it disappeared, and we never saw it again. Honestly, I mean, we didn't know until several weeks later. During the dispute, we ordered two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. The owner handled it at that stage. He admitted the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. I still think it was odd that he also claimed we were partly at fault because we hadn't been friendly enough to the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit-card company, and eventually we got a credit.
